outcome: M(10) and higher Dedekind numbers remain exactly uncomputed since 26 January 2024; two 2026 preprints produced statistical (non-rigorous) estimates of M(10) through M(15) using Monte Carlo / Markov-chain layer-ratio methods, narrowing where the true values plausibly lie but not settling any of them.
summary: The bullet asks for the exact values of the Dedekind numbers M(n) for n ≥ 10; as of 26 January 2024 only M(n) for n ≤ 9 were known exactly (M(9) was computed in 2023, before the window, and is not itself in scope since the bullet is about n ≥ 10). Since the frozen date, no exact value of M(10) or any higher Dedekind number has been computed or claimed — this remains far beyond current computational reach (the gap between known rigorous lower and upper bounds for M(10) spans roughly 230 orders of magnitude). Two 2026 preprints move the needle on the surrounding mathematics without settling the question: 'Finite-n Estimate of Dedekind Numbers by Layer-Ratio Monte Carlo' (arXiv:2606.09795, submitted 2026-06-08, Chen/Feng/Wang/Chen/Zhang) gives a statistical estimate M(10) ≈ (8.9360 ± 0.0010)×10^78 using reversible fixed-layer Markov chains to estimate layer ratios; 'Statistical Estimation of higher Dedekind Numbers' (arXiv:2607.08446, Fihman/Van Hirtum/Plessl) extends this to statistical estimates of D(10) through D(15) with several algorithmic variants (pair matching, reference subsets, weight-layer branching). Both papers are explicit that these are statistical/Monte Carlo estimates, not exact values or even rigorous bounds — they narrow uncertainty about where the true value likely lies but do not constitute a resolution, a new proven bound, or a case of the problem being settled (an 'exact value' question is not advanced by a probabilistic point estimate, per the rule that existence/value questions move only when actually answered). I read both papers' abstracts and available body text and found no mention of any AI or machine-learning system contributing to the estimation methodology; the techniques described are traditional statistical/algorithmic (Markov chain Monte Carlo, combinatorial counting), not learned models. A GitHub issue (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures #2360) merely proposes formalizing the open problem statement in Lean/Mathlib for tracking purposes — it was itself generated by an AI agent in February 2026 as a repository-maintenance action, but it reports no mathematical progress and its 'AI agent' authorship is about issue-filing, not about producing any mathematics, so it does not count as AI involvement in the problem itself. I classified status as 'progress' rather than 'open' because the two 2026 papers represent an instructive advance in estimating quantities the bullet is directly about, even though no bound or exact value was proven — this is closer to the 'a bound moved, or an instructive incident' sense of progress than to true silence, though I flag this as a judgment call (see competing_reading).
competing_reading: One could argue this should be classified as plain 'open' with no_change_found true, since a statistical Monte Carlo point estimate is neither a proven bound nor a settled case — it does not change what a careful person would write in the bullet's entry (the exact value of M(10) is exactly as unknown now as in January 2024), and 'progress' risks conflating an estimate with a bound movement. I lean toward 'progress' because the statistical estimates are the first substantive quantitative narrowing of belief about M(10)–M(15) since the (in-window-irrelevant) 2023 M(9) computation, and because it is an instructive computational advance in methodology directly targeting this exact question, but 'open' / no_change_found is a defensible alternative reading.
what_would_settle_it: An exact computation of M(10) (or any n ≥ 10) verified by independent recomputation or expert digestion, or a rigorously proven (non-statistical) narrowing of the lower/upper bound gap, would move this further; either would need to appear as a peer-reviewed or expert-vetted result rather than a preprint estimate to reach 'resolved'.
